title: Watch each software release for problems with agents
summary: An engineer built a prototype where agents plan monitoring for each release and investigate alerts; he says it caught regressions in systems he didn't understand.
agent_role: One agent reads the service code and writes a monitoring plan; a fixed system runs that plan, and another agent investigates any triggered checks. Humans get escalations.
outcome: Author reports detecting regressions in unfamiliar systems with speed and precision he says was impossible a year ago.
what_they_did: Ben Congdon prototyped agent-driven monitoring around software releases and settings changes. An agent reads the service code and writes a plan for what to watch. A regular program runs that plan. A second agent digs into anything that trips, and hands off to a person when needed.
how_it_went: He says even the early version caught problems in systems he knew nothing about, faster and more accurately than he could before.
worth_knowing: He found a pure agent loop worked worse. Having the agent write a monitoring plan that a plain program runs gave cleaner signals and used far fewer tokens.
prompt: Read the code for [service name] and the change in [release or config change]. Write a monitoring plan for the next [hours] after it goes live: which metrics and log lines to watch, normal ranges, and what counts as a problem. Save it as a file I can run on a schedule. When a check trips, investigate using [your logs and metrics tool], summarize the likely cause and evidence, and message me before taking any action like rolling back.

curation.rationale: A practitioner describes a working prototype that plans, runs and investigates release monitoring with agents and gives useful design lessons. There are no numbers or code, so it lands at worth-a-look.
